text.paragraph: Primary care visit for low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite, and weight loss over three months after several bereavements. Concerns: Heavy-hearted, sleeping about four hours a night, with no appetite, and her clothes are loose; she sometimes wishes she would not wake up; She fears that any word of her illness would leak and unsettle the country, and does not want to be seen as unfit for her office; Chewing is painful with her old partial denture, so she eats soft food and little of it. [S]

tr.td: Low mood, sleeplessness (about four hours a night), poor appetite, and unintended loss of 3.5 kg (6 percent) over three months, after bereavements and in a demanding public role; under evaluation for depression and medical causes
S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, echoing the documented low spirits and poor appetite of her last months; superseded by the depression diagnosis at the second visit.
Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate (PHQ-9 17 and GDS-15 10 at intake), in an older woman after bereavements; medical causes excluded

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. Her deep melancholy, sleeplessness, and refusal of food in her last months are documented (D); calling them major depression is a modern reading, and no diagnosis was made in her lifetime.

tr.td: Primary care visit for low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite, and weight loss over three months after several bereavements
Two-week review of results, diagnosis of major depression, start of treatment, and geriatric psychiatry consultation
Four-week depression treatment review with a sodium check
Same-day sick visit for a sore throat and low-grade fever

Workup for medical causes of low mood and weight loss: blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, albumin, TSH, vitamin B12, and folate; MoCA cognitive screen; medication review (stop the over-the-counter diphenhydramine sleep aid); dental examination; age-appropriate cancer screening confirmed up to date

Suicide-risk assessment and collaborative safety plan: warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; medicines kept by her maid; safety reviewed at every visit
Geriatric psychiatry consultation to confirm the diagnosis, review grief, cognition, and safety, and advise on antidepressant choice and psychotherapy for an older adult

Shared decision on treatment: combined interpersonal psychotherapy, focused on grief, and a second-generation antidepressant; she chose sertraline, starting at 25 mg for a week, then 50 mg, with a review every two to four weeks and a dose increase if she is not in remission by about twelve weeks; no tricyclics, paroxetine, or other strongly anticholinergic drugs
Weekly individual interpersonal psychotherapy with the clinic psychologist, in private sessions at the end of the day, for about 16 sessions

Sleep: stop diphenhydramine; cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (sleep window, stimulus control, a fixed rising time, no long naps, and worry time early in the evening); no benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or sedating antihistamines
Nutrition: three small meals and two snacks a day, an oral nutrition supplement twice a day, weight at every visit, and a dental review for the painful partial denture

Falls: Timed Up and Go and orthostatic blood pressure now and again if an antidepressant is started, since SSRIs raise fall risk in older adults; home safety review with her staff; an exercise class for balance and strength

Measurement-based care: PHQ-9 at every visit and at least monthly and GDS-15 monthly; if an SSRI is started, a sodium check two to four weeks later; continue any treatment that works for at least six to twelve months after remission
Privacy: chart access restricted to her care team, appointments at the end of the clinic day, results given in person, and nothing released without her written consent
Medical causes of low mood and weight loss excluded by the second visit
Blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, albumin, TSH, vitamin B12, folate, and MoCA normal; diphenhydramine stopped
Response (PHQ-9 down by at least 50 percent) by twelve weeks of treatment, then remission (PHQ-9 below 5)
PHQ-9 8 at seven weeks of sertraline, 53 percent below baseline; remission not yet reached
No passive or active suicidal thoughts
Passive death wish at intake only; PHQ-9 item 9 scored 0 from the second visit
Sleep at least six hours most nights without hypnotics
About five and a half hours by seven weeks with CBT for insomnia
Weight back to at least 55 kg, with a comfortable denture
53.4 kg at seven weeks; new denture being made

list.item: Independent in all activities of daily living; still carrying out her duties, but she postpones audiences, reads papers without taking them in, and has given up music and riding [S]
Thin, upright, carefully dressed and made up; formal and guarded at first, then candid; speech slow and quiet; frequent sighs; good eye contact [S]

Mood "heavy at heart"; affect constricted and tearful when she speaks of those who have died; thought process linear; a passive wish not to wake up on some mornings, with no intent, plan, or preparatory behavior; no psychotic features; MoCA 27; insight and judgment good [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 2026-01-12: current ideation present, intent absent, plan absent. Passive death wish only (C-SSRS screen: wish to be dead, no active thoughts, intent, plan, or behavior; no past attempt). Outpatient care with a collaborative safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and the clinic number, medicines kept by her maid, and review in two weeks [S]
